questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: Which four cranial bones articulate at the H-shaped sutural junction known as the pterion?
options: Frontal, parietal, squamous temporal, and greater wing of sphenoid
Parietal, occipital, mastoid temporal, and sphenoid body
Temporal, zygomatic, lesser wing of sphenoid, and ethmoid
questions.explain: The pterion is the weak H-shaped sutural junction on the lateral skull where the frontal, parietal, squamous part of the temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid bones meet directly over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.

open.q: Name the four skull bones that meet at the pterion on the lateral aspect of the cranium.
accept: frontal, parietal, squamous temporal, greater wing of sphenoid

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: Which structures pass through the foramen ovale in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone?
options: Mandibular nerve (V3), accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve and emissary vein
Maxillary nerve (V2) and artery of pterygoid canal
Middle meningeal artery and meningeal V3 branch
Ophthalmic nerve (V1) and ocular motor nerves
questions.explain: The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (CN V3), accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve (occasionally via canaliculus innominatus), and an emissary vein (mnemonic: MALE).

open.q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve exits the middle cranial fossa through the foramen ovale?

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: Which structure passes through the foramen spinosum of the sphenoid bone?
options: Middle meningeal artery and meningeal branch of V3
Internal carotid artery and sympathetic plexus
questions.explain: Located posterolateral to the foramen ovale, the foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery, middle meningeal vein, and the recurrent meningeal branch (nervus spinosus) of CN V3.

open.q: Name the major dural artery that enters the middle cranial fossa through the foramen spinosum.

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: Which cranial nerves exit the posterior cranial fossa through the jugular foramen alongside the internal jugular vein?
options: Glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), and accessory (CN XI) nerves
Facial (CN VII) and vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) nerves
Hypoglossal (CN XII) and vagus (CN X) nerves
Oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), and abducens (CN VI) nerves
questions.explain: The jugular foramen transmits the inferior petrosal sinus, CN IX, CN X, CN XI, and the sigmoid sinus continuing as the internal jugular vein.

open.q: Which three cranial nerves traverse the jugular foramen together with the internal jugular vein?

questions.sub: Scalp and Face
questions.q: Which layer of the scalp is known clinically as the 'danger area of the scalp' because emissary veins here communicate with the diploic veins and dural venous sinuses?
questions.explain: The 4th layer (loose areolar connective tissue) permits free movement of the scalp proper over the pericranium, allows blood or fluid to track down into the eyelids, and contains valveless emissary veins connecting to intracranial venous sinuses.

open.q: Which of the five layers of the scalp is termed the danger area of the scalp because infections within it can spread via emissary veins to the dural venous sinuses?

questions.sub: Scalp and Face
questions.q: Why do superficial lacerations of the scalp bleed profuse amounts of blood even when relatively small?
options: Fibrous septa tether scalp arteries, limiting retraction and vasospasm
Scalp supply comes only from the internal carotid
Emissary veins carry high-pressure arterial blood
questions.explain: Blood vessels of the scalp run in the dense second subcutaneous connective tissue layer where fibrous septa hold their walls open when cut, preventing retraction and constriction.

open.q: Why do blood vessels in the dense connective tissue layer of the scalp fail to retract and constrict when lacerated?
accept: tethered to dense fibrous connective tissue
held open by dense connective tissue

questions.sub: Scalp and Face
questions.q: Which muscle of facial expression pierces the buccopharyngeal fascia, keeps food between the molar teeth during mastication, and is pierced by the parotid duct?
questions.explain: The buccinator is an accessory muscle of mastication innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII); it compresses the cheeks against the teeth and is pierced by the parotid (Stensen) duct opposite the upper second molar.

open.q: Name the muscle of facial expression in the cheek that is pierced by the parotid duct and innervated by the buccal branch of CN VII.

questions.sub: Scalp and Face
questions.q: Why can infections in the 'danger triangle of the face' (upper lip and nose) spread into the cavernous sinus to cause cavernous sinus thrombosis?
options: Facial veins communicate with the cavernous sinus via ophthalmic and pterygoid veins
Facial artery joins the internal carotid
Facial lymphatics drain into the subarachnoid space
The infraorbital nerve carries bacteria to the trigeminal ganglion
questions.explain: Valveless communications link the facial and angular veins to the superior ophthalmic vein and via the deep facial vein to the pterygoid venous plexus, both of which drain directly into the cavernous sinus.

open.q: Through which two venous pathways can infections from the upper lip and nose spread from the facial vein into the cavernous sinus?
accept: superior ophthalmic vein and pterygoid venous plexus

questions.sub: Parotid Region and Facial Nerve
questions.q: A 42-year-old man develops Bell palsy affecting the right facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen. Which clinical sign is expected on the right side of his face?
options: Inability to close the right eye and drooping of the right mouth angle
Loss of sensation over the right cheek
Right ptosis with a dilated pupil
questions.explain: A lower motor neuron lesion of CN VII at the stylomastoid foramen paralyzes all ipsilateral muscles of facial expression, including orbicularis oculi (causing lagophthalmos/inability to close the eye) and orbicularis oris/zygomaticus (drooping mouth).

open.q: Which muscle of the eyelid is paralyzed in a lower motor neuron facial nerve lesion, preventing tight eye closure?

questions.sub: Parotid Region and Facial Nerve
questions.q: From superficial to deep within the substance of the parotid gland, what is the anatomical order of the three major neurovascular structures?
options: Facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery
External carotid artery, retromandibular vein, facial nerve
Retromandibular vein, facial nerve, external carotid artery
Facial nerve, external carotid artery, retromandibular vein
questions.explain: Within the parotid gland, the facial nerve and its pes anserinus lie most superficially, the retromandibular vein lies in the intermediate plane, and the external carotid artery lies deepest.

open.q: State the order of the facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery from superficial to deep inside the parotid gland.
accept: facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery

questions.sub: Parotid Region and Facial Nerve
questions.q: Postganglionic secretomotor parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland originate in the otic ganglion and reach the gland by hitchhiking on which nerve?
questions.explain: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the inferior salivatory nucleus travel via CN IX -> tympanic nerve -> lesser petrosal nerve to synapse in the otic ganglion; postganglionic fibers join the auriculotemporal nerve to enter the parotid gland.

open.q: Which branch of the mandibular nerve conveys postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland?

questions.sub: Temporal, Infratemporal Fossae and Muscles of Mastication
questions.q: Which muscle of mastication is the ONLY one that depresses and protrudes the mandible to open the mouth?
questions.explain: The temporalis, masseter, and medial pterygoid all elevate the mandible to close the jaw, whereas bilateral contraction of the lateral pterygoid pulls the condylar head and articular disc anteriorly onto the articular tubercle to open the mouth.

open.q: Name the sole muscle of mastication responsible for depressing the mandible to open the mouth.

questions.sub: Temporal, Infratemporal Fossae and Muscles of Mastication
questions.q: Which nerve carries taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular ganglion?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve (branch of CN X)
questions.explain: The chorda tympani arises from CN VII in the facial canal, crosses the tympanic membrane, exits via the petrotympanic fissure, and joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa to supply taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

open.q: Name the branch of the facial nerve that joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa to carry taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

questions.sub: Temporal, Infratemporal Fossae and Muscles of Mastication
questions.q: Which branch of the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery enters the mandibular foramen to supply the lower teeth and chin?
questions.explain: The first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery gives off five branches entering bony foramina: deep auricular, anterior tympanic, middle meningeal, accessory meningeal, and inferior alveolar arteries.

open.q: Which branch of the first part of the maxillary artery accompanies the inferior alveolar nerve into the mandibular canal?

questions.sub: Neck Triangles and Deep Cervical Fascia
questions.q: Which muscles form the boundaries of the posterior triangle of the neck?
options: Posterior SCM, anterior trapezius and middle clavicle
Anterior SCM, neck midline and mandible
questions.explain: The posterior triangle is bounded anteriorly by the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, posteriorly by the anterior border of the trapezius, and inferiorly by the middle one-third of the clavicle.

open.q: Name the three anatomical boundaries of the posterior triangle of the neck.
accept: posterior border of sternocleidomastoid, anterior border of trapezius, middle third of clavicle

questions.sub: Neck Triangles and Deep Cervical Fascia
questions.q: Following a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck, a 30-year-old patient cannot shrug her right shoulder or abduct her right arm above 90 degrees. Which nerve was injured?
questions.explain: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) courses obliquely across the posterior triangle embedded in the fascial roof just deep to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, making it vulnerable during posterior triangle surgery and causing trapezius paralysis.

open.q: Which cranial nerve traverses the roof of the posterior triangle of the neck and is vulnerable to injury during cervical lymph node biopsy?

questions.sub: Neck Triangles and Deep Cervical Fascia
questions.q: At which vertebral level does the common carotid artery bifurcate into the internal and external carotid arteries within the carotid triangle?
options: Upper border of thyroid cartilage (about C3–C4)
questions.explain: The common carotid artery bifurcates at the level of the superior border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-C4), where the carotid sinus and carotid body are located.

open.q: At which cervical vertebral level (and corresponding laryngeal cartilage landmark) does the common carotid artery bifurcate?
accept: C3-C4 at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage

questions.sub: Neck Triangles and Deep Cervical Fascia
questions.q: Which three structures are enclosed within the carotid sheath?
options: Common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve
External carotid artery, external jugular vein, and phrenic nerve
Subclavian artery, subclavian vein, and brachial plexus
Internal carotid artery, sympathetic trunk, and hypoglossal nerve
questions.explain: The carotid sheath encloses the common and internal carotid arteries medially, the internal jugular vein laterally, and the vagus nerve (CN X) posteriorly between them (with the cervical sympathetic trunk lying outside, posterior to the sheath).

open.q: List the three main neurovascular structures enclosed inside the carotid sheath.
accept: common or internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve
carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve

questions.sub: Neck Triangles and Deep Cervical Fascia
questions.q: Which infrahyoid (strap) muscle is innervated by C1 fibers traveling via the hypoglossal nerve rather than by the ansa cervicalis?
questions.explain: The sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid are innervated by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3), whereas the thyrohyoid (and geniohyoid) receives C1 fibers carried directly by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

open.q: Which infrahyoid muscle is supplied directly by C1 fibers hitchhiking on the hypoglossal nerve instead of the ansa cervicalis?

questions.sub: Neck Triangles and Deep Cervical Fascia
questions.q: Infection spreading downward in the retropharyngeal space (between the buccopharyngeal fascia and alar fascia) can enter which thoracic compartment?
questions.explain: The retropharyngeal space extends from the skull base down into the superior/posterior mediastinum (and via the adjacent danger space down to the diaphragm), providing a conduit for deep neck infections to cause mediastinitis.

open.q: Into which thoracic region can deep neck infections descend via the retropharyngeal and danger spaces?

questions.sub: Root of the Neck and Thyroid/Parathyroid Glands
questions.q: Which three structures pass through the interscalene triangle between the anterior and middle scalene muscles?
options: Roots/trunks of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery
Vagus nerve and internal jugular vein
Thoracic duct and recurrent laryngeal nerve
questions.explain: The trunks of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, whereas the subclavian vein and phrenic nerve pass anterior to the anterior scalene muscle.

open.q: Which major artery and nerve plexus emerge between the anterior and middle scalene muscles?

questions.sub: Root of the Neck and Thyroid/Parathyroid Glands
questions.q: On the anterior surface of which muscle does the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) descend vertically in the neck beneath the prevertebral fascia?
questions.explain: The phrenic nerve crosses the anterior surface of the anterior scalene muscle from lateral to medial behind the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia before entering the thorax.

open.q: Along the anterior surface of which cervical muscle does the phrenic nerve descend from lateral to medial?

questions.sub: Root of the Neck and Thyroid/Parathyroid Glands
questions.q: During thyroidectomy, which nerve is closely related to the superior thyroid artery near the apex of the thyroid lobe and is endangered if the artery is ligated too close to the gland?
questions.explain: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs alongside the superior thyroid artery near the superior pole of the thyroid gland (before diverging medially to innervate cricothyroid); ligating the artery close to the gland can damage it, causing loss of high-pitched vocal projection.

open.q: Which nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery at the upper pole of the thyroid lobe and innervates the cricothyroid muscle?
accept: external branch of superior laryngeal nerve

questions.sub: Root of the Neck and Thyroid/Parathyroid Glands
questions.q: Which nerve lies in the tracheoesophageal groove closely intertwined with branches of the inferior thyroid artery near the lower pole of the thyroid gland?
questions.explain: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in or near the tracheoesophageal groove close to the posterior aspect of the thyroid lobe and the inferior thyroid artery before entering the larynx beneath the inferior constrictor.

open.q: Which nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove in close relation to the inferior thyroid artery and the posterior surface of the thyroid gland?

questions.sub: Root of the Neck and Thyroid/Parathyroid Glands
questions.q: Why does the thyroid gland move upward during swallowing?
options: Pretracheal fascia and suspensory ligament attach it to the larynx
The hypoglossal nerve lifts it during tongue movement
The superior pole attaches to the styloid process
questions.explain: The pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia splits to enclose the thyroid gland (forming its false capsule and the suspensory ligament of Berry) and attaches above to the hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilages, pulling the gland upward during deglutition.

open.q: Which layer of deep cervical fascia invests the thyroid gland and attaches it to the laryngeal cartilages so that it moves during swallowing?

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: Which extrinsic muscle of the tongue protrudes the tongue forward and depresses its central part, and is used clinically to test hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) integrity?
questions.explain: The genioglossus (supplied by CN XII) pulls the tongue anteriorly; in unilateral CN XII palsy, the unopposed healthy genioglossus pushes the protruded tongue toward the paralyzed (lesioned) side.

open.q: Name the extrinsic tongue muscle that protrudes the tongue anteriorly and is tested when asking a patient to stick out their tongue.

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: Which muscle of the tongue or soft palate is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve, CN X) rather than the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)?
questions.explain: All intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue are innervated by CN XII except palatoglossus, which is developmentally a soft palate muscle innervated by CN X via the pharyngeal plexus.

open.q: Which extrinsic muscle of the tongue is innervated by the vagus nerve (pharyngeal plexus) instead of the hypoglossal nerve?

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: Which nerve provides BOTH general somatic sensation and taste sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue?
questions.explain: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies both general sensation and special visceral sensation (taste) to the posterior one-third of the tongue and the circumvallate papillae.

open.q: Which cranial nerve carries both general sensation and taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue?

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: Which tensor muscle of the soft palate hooks around the pterygoid hamulus and is innervated by the mandibular nerve (CN V3)?
questions.explain: All muscles of the soft palate are innervated by the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus except tensor veli palatini, which is supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid from CN V3.

open.q: Name the soft palate muscle that hooks around the pterygoid hamulus and is uniquely innervated by the mandibular nerve (CN V3).

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: In which triangular fossa on the lateral wall of the oropharynx does the palatine tonsil reside?
options: Tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
questions.explain: The palatine tonsil sits in the tonsillar sinus (fossa) bounded anteriorly by the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar) and posteriorly by the palatopharyngeal arch (posterior pillar).

open.q: Name the two mucosal arches that bound the tonsillar fossa containing the palatine tonsil anteriorly and posteriorly.

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: Which artery provides the main arterial blood supply to the palatine tonsil and is the most common source of severe hemorrhage following tonsillectomy?
options: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
questions.explain: While five arteries contribute to the tonsillar bed, the tonsillar branch of the facial artery pierces the superior constrictor to enter the inferior pole of the palatine tonsil as its main blood supply (alongside the paratonsillar vein).

open.q: From which major branch of the external carotid artery does the main tonsillar artery supplying the palatine tonsil arise?

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: Which structures pass through the gap between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscles?
options: Stylopharyngeus muscle and glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels
Recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal vessels
Auditory tube and tensor veli palatini
questions.explain: Between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors pass the stylopharyngeus muscle, glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), and stylohyoid ligament. Between the middle and inferior constrictors pass the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels.

open.q: Name the muscle and cranial nerve that enter the pharynx by passing through the gap between the superior and middle constrictor muscles.

questions.sub: Larynx
questions.q: Which laryngeal cartilage is the ONLY complete cartilaginous ring encircling the airway?
questions.explain: The signet-ring-shaped cricoid cartilage at the C6 vertebral level forms the only complete ring of cartilage in the respiratory tract, making it vital for maintaining airway patency.

open.q: Name the signet-ring-shaped laryngeal cartilage at the C6 level that forms the only complete cartilaginous ring around the airway.

questions.sub: Larynx
questions.q: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is the ONLY abductor of the vocal folds, widening the rima glottidis during inspiration?
questions.explain: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle rotates the arytenoid cartilages laterally to abduct the vocal folds and open the rima glottidis; bilateral paralysis leads to life-threatening airway obstruction.

open.q: Name the sole intrinsic muscle of the larynx that abducts the vocal folds to open the rima glottidis.

questions.sub: Larynx
questions.q: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle tenses and elongates the vocal folds to raise vocal pitch and is innervated by the external laryngeal nerve?
questions.explain: All intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except the cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to tense the vocal ligaments.

open.q: Which intrinsic muscle of the larynx tenses the vocal folds and is the only laryngeal muscle innervated by the external laryngeal nerve?

questions.sub: Larynx
questions.q: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa ABOVE the vocal folds and mediates the afferent limb of the cough reflex?
questions.explain: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery to provide sensory innervation above the vocal folds, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below the vocal folds.

open.q: Name the sensory nerve that pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to innervate the laryngeal mucosa superior to the vocal folds.
accept: internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

questions.sub: Larynx
questions.q: An emergency airway (cricothyrotomy) is performed in an adult with acute upper airway obstruction. Through which avascular membrane in the anterior midline is the incision made?
questions.explain: A needle or surgical cricothyrotomy pierces the superficial median cricothyroid ligament between the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage and the arch of the cricoid cartilage, avoiding major blood vessels and the vocal cords.

open.q: Through which midline ligament between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages is an emergency cricothyrotomy performed?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: Into which meatus of the lateral nasal wall does the nasolacrimal duct open?
questions.explain: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac into the anterior part of the inferior nasal meatus, beneath the inferior nasal concha.

open.q: Into which nasal meatus does the nasolacrimal duct open inferior to the inferior nasal concha?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: Why is the maxillary sinus particularly prone to chronic infection and fluid retention compared to the other paranasal sinuses?
options: Its high medial ostium makes drainage depend on mucociliary clearance
Its ostium lies on the floor, causing dependent pooling
It drains into the inferior meatus
questions.explain: The maxillary ostium is located near the roof of the maxillary sinus opening into the hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus, preventing passive gravity drainage when upright.

open.q: Into which groove of the middle nasal meatus does the ostium of the maxillary sinus open?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: Which extraocular muscle passes through a fibrocartilaginous trochlea on the superomedial orbital margin and is innervated by the trochlear nerve (CN IV)?
questions.explain: The superior oblique arises near the optic canal, passes through the trochlea on the frontal bone, and inserts onto the posterolateral sclera; supplied by CN IV, it intorts, depresses (especially when adducted), and abducts the eyeball (mnemonic: SO4, LR6, all else 3).

open.q: Name the extraocular muscle whose tendon loops through a pulley on the frontal bone and is supplied by the fourth cranial nerve.

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: A skull is examined from above. The examiner points to the midline junction between the sagittal and lambdoid sutures. Which craniometric landmark is indicated?
questions.explain: Lambda is the midline point where the sagittal and lambdoid sutures meet. Bregma is the junction of the sagittal and coronal sutures.

open.q: What is the craniometric landmark at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures?

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: A fracture through the optic canal threatens the optic nerve. Which additional structure normally passes through this canal?
questions.explain: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and ophthalmic artery from the middle cranial fossa into the orbit. The superior ophthalmic vein and the ocular motor nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure.

open.q: Which artery accompanies the optic nerve through the optic canal?

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: A lesion at the superior orbital fissure affects several nerves supplying extraocular muscles and sensation from the forehead and cornea. Which cranial nerve division is also transmitted through this fissure?
questions.explain: The superior orbital fissure transmits CN III, CN IV, CN VI, the ophthalmic division (V1) and the superior ophthalmic vein. V2 passes through foramen rotundum.

open.q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure?

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: A patient has sensory loss over the midface after a fracture involving the foramen rotundum. Which trigeminal division is most likely injured?
questions.explain: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) leaves the middle cranial fossa through foramen rotundum and supplies sensation to the midface, including the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip and upper teeth.

open.q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve passes through foramen rotundum?

questions.sub: Scalp and Face
questions.q: A newborn has weakness of several muscles of facial expression due to a developmental abnormality of the second pharyngeal arch. Which cranial nerve supplies muscles derived from this arch?
questions.explain: The muscles of facial expression develop from the second pharyngeal arch and are innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII). The first arch muscles are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

open.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles derived from the second pharyngeal arch?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: A patient has reduced lacrimation after injury to the greater petrosal nerve. The greater petrosal nerve joins which nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal?
questions.explain: The nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve, carrying preganglionic parasympathetic fibres, and the deep petrosal nerve, carrying postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus.

open.q: Which two nerves unite to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal?
accept: greater petrosal and deep petrosal nerves
greater petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: A lesion interrupts the parasympathetic pathway to the lacrimal gland before the fibres reach the pterygopalatine ganglion. Which cranial nerve carries these preganglionic secretomotor fibres?
questions.explain: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland travel in the facial nerve via the greater petrosal nerve and nerve of the pterygoid canal, then synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Postganglionic fibres reach the gland via V2, a communicating branch and the lacrimal nerve (V1).

open.q: Which cranial nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres destined for the lacrimal gland?

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: A thrombosis develops in the cavernous sinus. Which nerve is especially vulnerable because it runs within the venous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery rather than in its lateral wall?
questions.explain: The abducens nerve (CN VI) runs within the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery. CN III, CN IV, V1 and V2 are located in the lateral wall of the sinus.

open.q: Which cranial nerve runs within the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery?

questions.sub: Scalp and Face
questions.q: A deep scalp laceration has divided the dense connective-tissue layer immediately deep to the skin. Which of the following lists the five layers of the scalp from superficial to deep?
options: Skin, dense connective tissue, aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue, pericranium
Skin, aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue, dense connective tissue, pericranium
Skin, superficial fascia, deep fascia, periosteum, dura
Skin, pericranium, aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue, dense connective tissue
questions.explain: The five scalp layers from superficial to deep are skin, dense connective tissue, epicranial aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue and pericranium. The loose areolar layer is the clinically important danger area because infection can spread through emissary veins.

open.q: List the five layers of the scalp from superficial to deep.
accept: skin, dense connective tissue, aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue, pericranium
skin connective tissue aponeurosis loose areolar tissue pericranium

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: On a midsagittal section of the cranial cavity, a venous sinus is seen running along the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri. Which sinus is this?
questions.explain: The superior sagittal sinus runs in the attached superior border of the falx cerebri. The inferior sagittal sinus runs in its free inferior border and joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus.

open.q: Which dural venous sinus runs in the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: A patient has chronic maxillary sinusitis. The surgeon identifies the natural opening of the maxillary sinus on its medial wall. Into which part of the lateral nasal wall does it drain?
options: Middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris
questions.explain: The maxillary sinus drains into the middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris. Its opening is relatively high on the medial wall, which contributes to poor drainage when the patient is upright.

open.q: Into which nasal meatus does the maxillary sinus drain?
accept: middle meatus via the hiatus semilunaris

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: A patient with posterior ethmoidal sinusitis has inflammation near the upper part of the lateral nasal wall. Into which meatus do the posterior ethmoidal air cells normally open?
questions.explain: The posterior ethmoidal air cells drain into the superior nasal meatus. The middle ethmoidal cells open on or near the bulla ethmoidalis in the middle meatus, while the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.

open.q: Into which nasal meatus do the posterior ethmoidal air cells drain?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: A patient develops recurrent anterior epistaxis. Examination identifies a vascular plexus on the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum where several arterial sources anastomose. What is this region called?
questions.explain: Kiesselbach area (Little's area) is a superficial arterial anastomosis on the anteroinferior nasal septum and is a common source of anterior epistaxis. It receives contributions from branches of the sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine and superior labial arteries.

open.q: What is the name of the arterial plexus on the anteroinferior nasal septum that commonly causes anterior epistaxis?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: A patient has hyperacusis after a lesion affecting the motor supply to tensor tympani. Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to this muscle?
questions.explain: Tensor tympani is supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3). Stapedius is supplied by the facial nerve.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the tensor tympani muscle?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: A patient has hyperacusis because the stapedius muscle is paralyzed. Which cranial nerve normally supplies this muscle?
questions.explain: Stapedius is innervated by a small branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). Its contraction dampens movements of the stapes; paralysis can cause hyperacusis.

open.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the stapedius muscle?

questions.sub: Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Orbit, and Ear
questions.q: A patient has vertigo due to damage to the vestibular division of the vestibulocochlear nerve. In which ganglion are the primary sensory cell bodies of these vestibular fibres located?
questions.explain: The primary sensory cell bodies of the vestibular division of CN VIII are located in the vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion. The sensory cell bodies of the cochlear division are in the spiral ganglion.

open.q: Where are the primary sensory cell bodies of the vestibular division of CN VIII located?

questions.sub: Larynx
questions.q: A patient undergoes thyroid surgery and subsequently loses sensation from the laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds. Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explain: The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds and motor innervation to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies sensation above the vocal folds.

open.q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds?

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: A patient protrudes the tongue and it deviates to the right. Which side of the hypoglossal nerve is most likely damaged?
options: Neither; deviation is caused by the vagus nerve
questions.explain: A unilateral lower motor neuron lesion of the hypoglossal nerve causes the protruded tongue to deviate toward the side of the lesion because the intact genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak side.

open.q: In a unilateral hypoglossal nerve lesion, toward which side does the protruded tongue deviate?
accept: toward the side of the lesion

questions.sub: Neck Triangles and Deep Cervical Fascia
questions.q: A patient presents with ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and reduced sweating over the face after a lesion near the cervical sympathetic trunk. Which syndrome is present?
questions.explain: Horner syndrome results from interruption of the sympathetic pathway to the head and classically produces ipsilateral mild ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. Apparent enophthalmos may also be described.

open.q: What syndrome causes ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis after interruption of the cervical sympathetic pathway?

questions.sub: Osteology of the Skull and Foramina
questions.q: A patient sustains a midfacial injury with a pyramidal fracture passing through the nasal bridge, medial orbital walls and maxillae. Which Le Fort fracture pattern is most consistent with this description?
questions.explain: Le Fort II is the pyramidal midface fracture pattern. It typically involves the nasal bridge, medial orbital walls, infraorbital rims and maxillae; Le Fort I is a low horizontal maxillary fracture, while Le Fort III separates the midface from the cranial base.

open.q: Which Le Fort fracture is classically described as a pyramidal fracture of the midface?

questions.sub: Orbit and Cavernous Sinus
questions.q: A patient develops loss of corneal sensation and a reduced corneal reflex after a lesion in the cavernous sinus. Which trigeminal division is most directly affected?
questions.explain: The ophthalmic division (V1) traverses the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and carries the afferent limb of the corneal reflex via the nasociliary branch.

open.q: Identify the structure or concept tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.sub: Orbit and Cavernous Sinus
questions.q: A patient has a dilated pupil and loss of accommodation following compression of the oculomotor nerve in the cavernous sinus. Which fibres have been interrupted?
options: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres destined for the ciliary ganglion
Postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion
General sensory fibres from the maxillary nerve
Branchial motor fibres to the muscles of mastication
questions.explain: The oculomotor nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus to the ciliary ganglion; interruption causes mydriasis and loss of accommodation.

open.q: Identify the structure or concept tested in this clinical scenario.
accept: preganglionic parasympathetic fibres destined for the ciliary ganglion

questions.sub: Face and Parotid Region
questions.q: During parotid surgery, a patient develops weakness of the lower lip on the operated side. Which facial nerve branch is most likely injured?
questions.explain: The marginal mandibular branch supplies muscles of the lower lip, including depressor anguli oris and depressor labii inferioris; injury causes asymmetry of lower-lip movement.

open.q: Identify the structure or concept tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.sub: Nasal Cavity and Paranasal Sinuses
questions.q: A posterior nosebleed is difficult to control and is traced to the sphenopalatine artery. This artery enters the nasal cavity through which opening?
questions.explain: The sphenopalatine artery, a terminal branch of the maxillary artery, enters the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen in the lateral nasal wall.

open.q: Identify the structure or concept tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.sub: Oral Cavity, Tongue, and Pharynx
questions.q: A patient loses taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but retains general touch sensation in that region. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
options: Lingual nerve proximal to chorda tympani union
questions.explain: Chorda tympani (facial nerve) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and joins the lingual nerve. General sensation is carried by the lingual nerve (V3).

open.q: Identify the structure or concept tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.sub: Orbit and cranial nerves
questions.q: A patient presents with ptosis, a dilated pupil and an eye positioned down and laterally. Which cranial nerve lesion best explains the combination?
questions.explain: A complete oculomotor nerve palsy affects levator palpebrae superioris, most extraocular muscles and parasympathetic fibres to the pupil, producing ptosis, a dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye.

open.q: Which cranial nerve lesion can cause ptosis, a dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye?

questions.sub: Neck and carotid sheath
questions.q: During thyroid surgery, the surgeon identifies the vagus nerve within the carotid sheath. Where does it normally lie relative to the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein?
options: Posteriorly, between the artery and vein
Medial to the common carotid artery and outside the sheath
questions.explain: The carotid sheath encloses the common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve. The vagus nerve typically lies posteriorly between the artery and vein.

open.q: Where is the vagus nerve located within the carotid sheath?
accept: Posteriorly between the carotid artery and internal jugular vein

questions.sub: Neck Triangles and Deep Cervical Fascia
questions.q: During an emergency examination, a clinician palpates the prominent anterior tubercle of a cervical transverse process and uses it as a landmark for compressing the common carotid artery. Which vertebral level is being palpated?
questions.explain: The anterior tubercle of the C6 transverse process is the carotid tubercle (Chassaignac tubercle). The common carotid artery can be compressed against it. This is a useful anatomical landmark in the lower neck.

open.q: Name the cervical vertebral level of the carotid (Chassaignac) tubercle.
